query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In compositionally complex high-entropy alloys (HEAs), exposure to service-relevant thermal aging combined with cyclic mechanical loading induces subtle changes in local chemical short-range order at grain boundaries. This ordering triggers the formation of nanoscale brittle clusters that act as fracture initiation sites—a mechanism distinct from the conventional segregation‐driven embrittlement in simpler alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous single-phase high-entropy alloy with a compositionally complex matrix and uniformly distributed elements, exhibiting high toughness and ductility.
generation.intervention: Subject samples to thermal aging at high temperatures (e.g., >0.5 T_m) combined with cyclic mechanical loading to induce stress concentrations.
generation.conditions: Service-like conditions including high-temperature exposure and cyclic (or dynamic) loading; for controlled comparison, similar treatments are applied to conventional alloys known to embrittle via grain-boundary segregation.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale brittle clusters or precipitates forming at or near grain boundaries, arising from local changes in chemical short-range order.
generation.mechanism: Under thermal and mechanical stress, small compositional redistributions in the complex matrix of the HEA promote a local transition in chemical ordering at grain boundaries. This transition leads to the nucleation of brittle clusters that lower the energy barrier for crack initiation, thereby shifting the mechanical behavior from ductile to brittle fracture modes. This differs from conventional alloys, where embrittlement typically arises from the accumulation of segregated species or coarse intermetallic phase precipitation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the initial homogeneous state, the HEA subjected to the intervention is expected to show measurable decreases in toughness and a higher propensity for brittle fracture. Microstructural analyses (such as TEM or atom probe tomography) should reveal the presence of the predicted nanoscale clusters at grain boundaries, a feature absent or less pronounced in comparable conventional alloys under the same loading conditions.
generation.baseline: As-annealed, homogeneous single-phase HEA with high toughness and ductility, lacking nanoscale brittle clusters at the grain boundaries.
generation.boundary: This mechanistic behavior is expected primarily under high temperatures (above ~0.5 T_m) and under cyclic/dynamic loadings; under low temperature or static loading conditions, the effect may not manifest, preserving the alloy's ductile characteristics.
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetics of the local chemical ordering, the exact composition of the nanoscale clusters, and their evolution under varied loading conditions remain not fully defined. There is also uncertainty regarding the potential role of minor impurities or residual stresses in the observed behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples with identical initial homogeneous microstructures. Subject one set to high-temperature thermal aging combined with cyclic mechanical loading, while keeping a control set under minimal or static load at the same temperature. Concurrently, perform a similar treatment on a conventional alloy with known segregation-induced embrittlement. Post-treatment, analyze the microstructure using TEM and atom probe tomography to detect the presence or absence of nanoscale clusters at the grain boundaries and measure fracture toughness tests to assess changes in mechanical behavior.
measurements: Atom probe tomography (APT) for chemical ordering and cluster detection
Comparative mechanical testing between HEA and conventional alloy samples
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA samples subjected to the intervention do not exhibit nanoscale brittle clusters or any significant local chemical ordering changes at grain boundaries compared to the baseline, and if the fracture toughness does not decrease (i.e., no transition from ductile to brittle behavior is observed), then the hypothesis is falsified.
